newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's exit from IMF not tied to tax - official.
newsitem.headline: Manila's exit from IMF not tied to tax - official.

text.p: Philippine Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said on Thursday the passage of the income tax reform bill was not a prerequisite to the country's exit from the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) 35 years of supervision.
"The present programme is a three-year programme. It ends in June. The exit that we are targetting, of course, will be at the end of the programme itself," de Ocampo said in a news conference.
He said the passage of the tax reform programme before the end of the month was essential in maintaining a fiscal surplus and increasing the domestic savings rate.
The Philippine Congress is currently deliberating on a bill that will widen the individual and corporate tax base, rationalise tax incentives and streamline tax administration.
"We are not passing a comprehensive tax reform programme just for the purpose of graduating from the IMF. That's just one of the effects," he said.

"It is important to have a good revenue stream. If it is passed, then the economy is in a good footing. If the economy is in a good footing, our likelihood of becoming sick man of Asia again is much less. And if you're not a sick man of Asia, you do not need a doctor," de Ocampo added.
IMF resident representative David Nellor said the passage of the bill will transform the economy into a self-sufficient one.

"A foundation for sustained growth is now being established and this provides genuine cause for celebration but also the need for vigilance to protect those gains. Passage of an effective tax reform is one essential element to strengthen that foundation for sustainable growth," Nellor said in his speech before a local Rotary club.
